claims.text: The initial refractory HEA is a single-phase MoNbTaW-type alloy produced by conventional melting and casting.
The conventionally cast refractory HEA has a typical coarse-grained microstructure.
Approximately 1–2 vol% nanoscale Y2O3 will be introduced into the refractory HEA.
Mechanical alloying followed by consolidation can produce a homogeneous Y2O3 dispersion in the HEA matrix.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Uniformly dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
A low-volume-fraction Y2O3 dispersion will not promote unwanted phase transformations.
Y2O3 particles pin moving dislocations and thereby increase yield strength.
Y2O3 particles trap or facilitate recombination of irradiation-generated vacancies and interstitials.
Defect trapping and recombination mitigate irradiation-induced defect accumulation and mechanical softening.
The dual strengthening and defect-sink functions preserve phase stability at high temperature and under irradiation.
The Y2O3-strengthened alloy will have higher yield strength than the oxide-free refractory HEA baseline.
The Y2O3-strengthened alloy will have greater resistance to irradiation-induced damage than the oxide-free baseline.
The Y2O3-strengthened alloy will retain phase stability and high-temperature mechanical properties.
The expected benefits apply at temperatures up to approximately 1000°C and irradiation doses up to approximately 10 dpa.
Oxide fractions above approximately 1–2 vol%, temperatures above 1000°C, or doses above 10 dpa may cause oxide coarsening or embrittlement.
Extended high-temperature exposure or higher irradiation doses may coarsen the Y2O3 particles and compromise mechanical reinforcement.
